title: Learning the Context of Errors: Black-Box Online Adaptation of Time Series Foundation Models
claim: Existing adaptation methods fall into three access-level paradigms; as models become closed APIs, only the gradient-free black-box paradigm remains feasible.
layout: Top timeline banner, then three stacked colored boxes; dashed divider separates prior from ours
description: A text-based taxonomy figure. A gray banner at the top shows a gradient dashed arrow running from 'Now: Open-Source / White-Box' in warm red-orange to 'Future: Maybe Close-Source/API/Commercialized / Requiring Black-Box (Gradient-Free)' in dark green. Beneath it are three rounded boxes with title tabs. A red-pink box on the left is 'Parameter Finetuning' and lists SOLID and DSOF. A blue box on the right is 'Grey-Box' and lists TAFAS, ADAPT-Z and δ-Adapter. A wide green box at the bottom is 'Black-Box (Gradient-Free)'. A dashed vertical line splits it into prior work ELF on the left and the authors' ORCA on the right. ORCA's insight ('Learning the Context of Error') is in bold italics. The colors follow the timeline gradient, and the eye goes first to the banner and then to the green ORCA box.
caption: Categorization of Time Series Online Adaptation Methods. Depending on the access level to the base model, existing approaches are grouped into three paradigms. In the coming era of commercialized TSFM APIs, only the Black-Box paradigm could provide a feasible solution.
abstract: The rapid evolution of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) has advanced zero-shot forecasting across diverse domains. Inspired by the current form of Large Language Models, future TSFMs may be offered as commercialized, closed-source API services. However, many existing online adaptation methods still rely on white-box access for parameter fine-tuning or gradient backpropagation. This paradigm mismatch raises a question: In black-box online adaptation for TSFMs, what should we learn? We answer this with an insight: the predictive errors of the base model are conditioned on both the input and output of the base model (i.e., the context of errors). To validate this insight, we propose ORCA (Online Residual Contextual Adaptation). We conduct extensive experiments across 5 state-of-the-art TSFMs and 8 datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, through ablation studies, we quantitatively analyze the impact of different adapter learning hypotheses on the final adaptation performance in black-box online adaptation. Code available at https://github.com/Fifthky/ORCA.
